intent: Expose the smallest stable set of operations a client needs and keep every decision that is likely to change — representation, algorithm, dependency — on the far side of that surface.
problem: Clients bind to the details of a collaborator, so changing how something is stored, computed or provided forces edits everywhere the thing is used, and the same knowledge is restated in every caller.
context: Abstraction and encapsulation are two halves of one move: abstraction is the interface you promise, encapsulation is the machinery you refuse to expose. Parnas's framing is the operative one — start from the list of design decisions that are likely to change and put one behind each interface. Data encapsulation (private fields plus accessors) is only one technique; the more powerful forms hide a data structure, an algorithm, a device, an external system, or the very existence of the variation.
benefits: A change-prone decision lives in one place and is edited there.
Clients are written against promises, not representations, so they survive rewrites.
Invariants can be enforced once, in the only place that can see the whole state.
Multiple implementations become possible because the contract does not mention the mechanism.
Test doubles can replace the whole collaborator because only the contract is visible.
tradeoffs: Every call pays an indirection: a virtual dispatch, an argument copy, a conversion.
Debuggers and loggers cannot see inside the abstraction, which slows diagnosis of exactly the problems that are hardest.
Accessors that merely forward to a private field are encapsulation in name only — the representation is still public knowledge.
Over-abstraction leaks the implementation anyway: a getter returning an internal slice, or an iterator over live mutable state.
Leaking abstractions are worse than none: once a client depends on a detail, tightening the surface is a breaking change.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 5 and performance 5 because every abstraction costs indirection; extensibility 9 and testability 9 are the payoff. coupling 9 = coupling is controlled and directional (strong inside, weak at the surface).

participants.responsibility: Uses only the abstraction; must not need to know the mechanism.
participants.notes: The client is the test of the abstraction: if it needs the implementation, the surface is wrong.

participants.responsibility: The stable promise that reveals unchanging aspects and hides varying ones.
participants.notes: Parnas/Britton: an abstract interface represents the assumptions common to all implementations.

participants.responsibility: The hidden design decision — data structure, algorithm, device, dependency.
participants.notes: If nothing in the module is likely to change, there is no secret to hide and the boundary is probably wrong.

use_cases: Replacing direct slice access with an iterator so the backing store can change.
Hiding an ORM session behind a repository so the domain model stops depending on the ORM.
Putting a timestamp source behind a clock interface so tests can control time.
Wrapping a third-party SDK so its error taxonomy never crosses the boundary.
Returning a copy or an immutable view instead of a reference to internal mutable state.
avoid_when: The data is a plain value that the client legitimately needs in full; wrapping it in accessors only adds ceremony.
The boundary would have one caller and one implementation forever — the abstraction will never be tested against reality.
Performance is measured to be dominated by the indirection in a documented hot path.
The "abstraction" is a thin passthrough that adds a name without hiding a decision.
pitfalls: Returning a reference or slice to internal mutable state — the encapsulation is one alias away from gone.
Getters that expose the exact structure (`getItems()[0].id`) so the client re-derives the representation.
Interface proliferation where each caller gets its own view and the implementation cannot satisfy them all.
Leaking an exception type from an implementation detail across the boundary.
Confusing data encapsulation with information hiding: private fields hide representation but not the algorithm or the dependency.

related_patterns_notes.encapsulate-collection: The tightest common case: hide a collection's representation behind a traversal interface.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Encapsulation applied to persistence — the storage strategy is the secret behind a collection-like interface.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: Encapsulation across a boundary you do not own: translate the foreign mechanism into your own contract.
related_patterns_notes.private-class-data: The C++ technique for removing a class's layout from the header, so clients cannot depend on it.

anti_patterns: Public mutable fields with getters and settors over the same field.
An interface whose methods return the internal collections directly.
A "Service" class exposing every collaborator as a public property.
An interface so wide it must be implemented once and mostly defaulted.
Abstraction that leaks: the second release exposes the implementation because the first contract was not designed.
design_principles: Begin with a list of difficult design decisions, or design decisions likely to change; design each module to hide one such decision (Parnas 1972).
Modules interact through abstract interfaces that reveal as little as possible about their inner workings.
An abstract interface must permit one implementation to be replaced by another without affecting other modules (Britton, Parker, Parnas 1981).
Information hiding is protected variation, not data encapsulation (Larman).
Knowledge of a module's implementation should not leak past its interface.
best_practices: Design the interface before the implementation, and write it from the client's point of view.
Return copies, immutable values or read-only views — never references to internal state.
Keep the interface free of implementation vocabulary (no `*_node`, `*_row`, `*_impl`).
If a client asks for a new method that exposes a detail, that detail belongs in the interface.
Use the encapsulation to enforce invariants in one place instead of validating at every call site.
Expect to change implementations, not interfaces; that asymmetry is what makes refactoring cheap.
